newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - C&W highlights shifting telecoms alliances.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - C&W highlights shifting telecoms alliances.

text.p: Telecommunications group Cable and Wireless Plc appeared set to abandon its alliance with two German utilities on Monday, a move analysts said could shift the balance of power in Europe's biggest telecoms market.

C&W's departure from the alliance would weaken the position of Veba AG and RWE AG on the German telecoms market less than 12 months before markets are fully opened and competition to monopoly Deutsche Telekom is set to begin in earnest.
Officials close to the German utilities said senior executives of C&W, Veba AG and RWE AG were meeting in Germany, but the companies would not confirm a meeting was taking place.
"We hope we will be able to make a statement today," said a spokeswoman for Vebacom, the C&W/Veba joint venture.
C&W and Veba formed a strategic alliance in 1995, with Veba taking a 10.5 percent stake in the British telecoms group and C&W taking 45 percent of a joint venture called Vebacom GmbH.
Last year, the two companies agreed to bring RWE on board and after months of negotiations drew up the final contracts two weeks ago but C&W has declined to sign them.
There are several international ventures competing for the business of global enterprises.

The main ventures are the Concert merger of British Telecom and MCI of the U.S., the Global One venture of France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and Sprint, AT&T-led World Partners and Europe's Unisource NV.

Should C&W bail out of the Vebacom alliance, it would weaken the competitive position of Veba and RWE on the German telecoms market, not only in relation to Deutsche Telekom but also to other newcomers like Mannesmann.
Mannesmann is Germany's leading cellular phone operator and is the industrial leader in the Arcor group that includes the German railway, AT&T, Deutsche Bank and Unisource NV.
"This would mean a considerable delay for Veba and RWE. Mannesmann is already positioned in the market, which means it can do business," said BHF Bank analyst Hermann Reith.

Veba and RWE have said they would continue to build their alliance, but departure of C&W would leave them without international services and products to offer, which is becoming increasingly important as the telecoms market becomes global.
Some analysts speculated that C&W's withdrawal from Vebacom would set the stage for Veba and RWE to link up with the Viag Interkom venture of utility Viag AG and British Telecom.

While such a deal would not be without complications -- RWE left the Interkom alliance to join Veba and C&W last July -- in the longer term it would lead to a consolidation on the German market and a strengthening of Telekom's challengers.
"Initially it would mean disarray among the competition and that would be good for Telekom," said Tim Hirst, analyst with Kleinwort Benson, the investment arm of Dresdner Bank.
"But then it would focus competitive efforts and that would be negative for Telekom," he added.

The trouble between Veba and C&W came about after Richard Brown was appointed C&W chief executive last year. Brown, a former Sprint executive, is believed to be exploring a possible alliance with Global One.

C&W and Global One would fit well together. C&W has a strong presence in Asia and Britain with its holdings in Hong Kong Telecom and its Mercury subsidiary. But uncertainties remain about the attitude of the Chinese government after it takes control of Hong Kong later this year.
Such an alliance could finally create a global telecoms group with a strong presence in triade U.S.-Europe-Asia and increase Global One's attraction to multinational businesses.

C&W's advances toward Global One come as British Telecom and Japan's NTT hold talks. While both companies have played down their meetings, speculation is rife that they could produce some form of cooperation.
Regardless of where the wheel stops turning, analysts said these developments highlight how fluid telecoms alliances are.

"Germany is just the microcosm for the global market," said Hirst. "The BT/MCI merger is perhaps the most secure of them all right now, but we are going to see a lot of change and shuffling of relationships."
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097150
